common_name: Bluecrisp Blueberry (Crisp-Fleshed University of Florida Southern Highbush)

planting.note: Plant dormant, container-grown bushes in late winter to early spring in highly acidic, well-drained soil amended with pine bark; Bluecrisp is a low-chill (roughly 400-hour) University of Florida release well suited to north Florida and south Georgia winters.

directions: Plant in acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.2) amended generously with pine bark or peat, keeping the shallow root zone consistently moist but never waterlogged. Bluecrisp was bred by the University of Florida for an unusually firm, crisp bite that holds up well through shipping, on a vigorous, semi-upright bush with a low chilling requirement suited to mild Gulf Coast winters. It shows useful field tolerance to Phytophthora root rot and Botryosphaeria stem blight, two diseases that limit many older highbush selections in the Southeast, though it is only partially self-fruitful and yields best with a different southern highbush cultivar planted nearby for cross-pollination. Feed with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and again lightly after harvest, and renew the planting each winter by removing the oldest, least productive canes.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Southern Highbush Blueberry Cultivars from the University of Florida (HS1245)
University of Georgia Extension — Blueberry Cultivars for Georgia

common_name: Magnus Blueberry (Early Hand-Harvest University of Florida Southern Highbush)

planting.note: Plant dormant, container-grown bushes in late winter to early spring in highly acidic, pine-bark-amended soil; Magnus is a University of Florida release with a somewhat higher chilling requirement than most southern highbush, best suited to north-central Florida and the coastal Gulf South.

directions: Plant in strongly acidic (pH 4.5-5.2), well-drained soil amended with pine bark, and mulch heavily to keep roots cool and evenly moist through the growing season. Magnus was released by the University of Florida as an early-season, hand-harvest cultivar prized for large, firm berries comparable in size to Emerald, though the fruit is not firm enough to hold up under mechanical harvesting equipment. It has performed consistently across seasons and under both hydrogen-cyanamide and non-cyanamide bud-break management, making it a dependable choice for growers who apply dormancy-breaking sprays as well as those who do not. Because its chilling requirement runs a bit higher than many low-chill southern highbush releases, it rewards sites with reliably cool winters within the Gulf Coast growing region rather than the very mildest microclimates.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Southern Highbush Blueberry Cultivars from the University of Florida (HS1245)
University of Georgia Extension — Blueberry Cultivars for Georgia

common_name: Patrecia Blueberry (Early Firm-Fruited University of Florida Southern Highbush)

planting.note: Plant dormant, container-grown bushes in late winter to early spring in highly acidic, pine-bark-amended soil; Patrecia is a University of Florida release, a cross of 'Star' and 'Springhigh', bred for north-central Florida and the wider Gulf Coast low-chill blueberry region.

directions: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5-5.2), well-drained soil amended with pine bark, spacing plants for the upright, spreading habit this cultivar develops as it matures. Patrecia was developed from a cross of 'Star' and 'Springhigh' and released by the University of Florida for its early-to-mid season ripening, large and very uniformly ripening berries, and late bloom that reduces exposure to spring freeze damage compared with earlier-flowering cultivars. The fruit's picking scar runs larger than ideal and can tear during harvest, so growers hand-pick rather than machine-harvest this selection, and yields respond well to a hydrogen-cyanamide bud-break program. Fertilize with an acid-forming blend in early spring, mulch heavily with pine bark to hold soil moisture and acidity, and remove the oldest canes each dormant season to keep the bush renewing itself.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Southern Highbush Blueberry Cultivars from the University of Florida (HS1245)
University of Georgia Extension — Blueberry Cultivars for Georgia

common_name: Georgia Dawn Blueberry (Very-Early-Season University of Georgia Southern Highbush)

planting.note: Plant dormant, container-grown bushes in late winter to early spring in highly acidic, pine-bark-amended soil; Georgia Dawn (originally trialed as TH-819) is a University of Georgia release valued for opening the harvest earlier than almost any other southern highbush cultivar.

directions: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5-5.2), well-drained soil amended with pine bark and mulched heavily to buffer soil temperature and moisture through the Gulf Coast growing season. Bred by the University of Georgia from a cross of 'Star' and a southern highbush selection, Georgia Dawn is grown chiefly for its very early ripening, flavor, and good berry color, scar, and firmness that let growers reach market ahead of most other cultivars. Its flowers open very early in the season, so sites prone to late-winter cold snaps need frost or freeze protection during bloom to avoid crop loss. Feed with an acid-forming fertilizer after bloom and again lightly post-harvest, and thin out old canes each dormant season to keep young, fruitful wood coming.
sources: University of Georgia CAES — Blueberry Variety Releases from the University of Georgia

common_name: Pinnacle Blueberry (Early Large-Fruited NC State/USDA Southern Highbush)

planting.note: Plant dormant, container-grown bushes in late winter to early spring in highly acidic, pine-bark-amended soil; Pinnacle is a joint NC State University/USDA-ARS release with a moderate-to-higher chilling requirement, best suited to the cooler edge of the southern blueberry belt.

directions: Plant in acidic, well-drained, organic-matter-rich soil amended with pine bark, since Pinnacle performs best on the kind of moisture-retentive 'blueberry soils' historically favored for highbush production. Developed jointly by NC State University and USDA-ARS breeders, Pinnacle is grown for early ripening, large, light-blue, firm berries with excellent shelf life that hold up well to shipping and handling. The self-fertile flowers produce abundant pollen and the semi-upright bush is only moderately vigorous, so routine pruning of older wood each winter helps keep new fruiting canes coming without letting the plant become overcrowded. Fertilize with an acid-forming blend in early spring and maintain a thick pine-bark or pine-straw mulch to hold the soil acidity and moisture this cultivar needs.
sources: NC State University Blueberry Genetics & Genomics Laboratory — Pinnacle cultivar profile
North Carolina Blueberry Council — New Southern Highbush Cultivar Pinnacle

common_name: Pender Blueberry (Machine-Harvest NC State Southern Highbush)

planting.note: Plant dormant, container-grown bushes in late winter to early spring in highly acidic, pine-bark-amended soil; Pender is an older NC State University release bred primarily for machine-harvested processing fruit rather than fresh-market hand-picking.

directions: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5-5.2), well-drained soil amended with pine bark, spacing bushes to allow airflow and eventual mechanical harvest access down the row. Released by North Carolina State University's blueberry breeding program, Pender ripens early to mid-season with smaller berries than most modern fresh-market southern highbush cultivars, reflecting its partial wild highbush parentage and its intended use for processing rather than fresh sale. It fits growers who want a dependable, mechanically harvestable cultivar for juice, jam, or IQF processing rather than premium hand-picked fruit. Feed with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring, keep a heavy organic mulch in place, and prune out the oldest canes each dormant season to sustain productive new growth.
sources: NC State University Blueberry Genetics & Genomics Laboratory — Pender cultivar profile
University of Georgia Extension — Blueberry Cultivars for Georgia
North Carolina Cooperative Extension — Growing Blueberries in North Carolina
